analysis.investment_thesis: Anup Engineering is a respectable niche process equipment manufacturer with genuine growth (revenue CAGR 24.5%, profit CAGR 22.4%) and adequate returns (ROE 18.9%), but it is a capital-intensive industrial business — precisely the kind I avoid — priced at a full 34.8x P/E and 22x EV/EBITDA with free cash flow turning sharply negative (-51 Cr in FY25). At this price, I'm paying for perfection in a business that doesn't offer the pricing power or moat durability I require.
key_strengths: Strong revenue momentum: 24.5% revenue CAGR and operating income growing from INR 70 Cr to 168 Cr over 5 years signals real demand
Manageable leverage: D/E of 0.25 and a long history of near-zero debt until recently shows conservative financial culture
Niche specialization: technology products (helix changers, EMBaffle exchangers) and multi-sector exposure (oil & gas, hydrogen, pharma) create modest switching costs
key_risks: Capital intensity trap: Capex averaged INR 51 Cr/yr over last 3 years; FCF turned -51 Cr in FY25 despite INR 118 Cr reported net profit — a classic warning sign
Valuation leaves no margin of safety: 34.8x P/E and 6.36x P/B for a cyclical industrial equipment maker is pricing in flawless execution
Cyclicality of end markets: oil & gas and petrochemicals capex is notoriously lumpy; an investment cycle downturn could rapidly compress earnings and expose the high multiple
red_flags: FY25 operating cash flow turned negative (-7 Cr) while net profit was INR 118 Cr — a large working capital deterioration that demands explanation
Borrowings jumped from zero in FY22 to INR 158 Cr by FY25 even as cash fell to just INR 3 Cr, suggesting the growth is being funded by debt and equity rather than internal generation
Gross margin reported at 3.79% suggests extreme raw-material pass-through business with limited pricing power on input costs
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Anup Engineering operates in a respectable niche — custom process equipment for energy and chemical industries — and the 5-year operating track record is genuinely solid. Revenue has compounded at 24.5%, operating income at 19.1%, and ROE sits at a reasonable 18.9%. The company has technology differentiation through licensed products and serves industries where quality and certifications create modest barriers. These are positives, and I can see why the market has re-rated this business sharply.

However, the FY25 cash flow statement tells a cautionary tale. Net profit of INR 118 Cr produced operating cash flow of negative INR 7 Cr — a gap of INR 125 Cr that is almost certainly working capital (receivables/inventory build) associated with a large order book ramp. Free cash flow was -51 Cr. Meanwhile borrowings have quietly risen to INR 158 Cr while cash shrank to INR 3 Cr. This is not a business generating cash; it is consuming it to grow. For a manufacturer of bespoke heavy equipment sold to large industrial clients, long cash conversion cycles are structural, not temporary. At 34.8x trailing P/E and over 22x EV/EBITDA, the market is pricing this like a high-quality compounder, but I am being asked to pay a premium for a capital-hungry industrial cyclical where every rupee of profit growth requires meaningful reinvestment and working capital. That is not the kind of business I like to own at any price, and certainly not at this price.
